senses: A period of time between the end of one monarch's reign and the accession of their successor.
A break in continuity; a gap, an intermission.
A period of time between when a minister or pastor leaves a church and when a new one is installed.
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin interrēgnum, from inter- (prefix meaning ‘between’) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁entér (“between”)) + rēgnum (“reign; royal power”) (nominalized from the neuter of *rēgnus, from rēx (“king; ruler”, oblique stem rēg-) + -nus (suffix forming adjectives), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ- (“to righten; to straighten”)). The plural form interregna is a learned borrowing from Latin interrēgna.
examples: The Sasanian Interregnum of 628–632

Between the end of the Fowler régime in 1931 and the advent of Stanier in 1932, there was a short interregnum during which Ernest Lemon was in charge, with Ernest Beames as his principal aide-de-camp.

All I know is that you could, if you wanted to, find the answers to all sorts of difficult questions buried in that terrible war-torn interregnum between the first pubic hair and the first soiled Durex.

senses: Structure with roof for shade but with no walls used for public gatherings. A pavilion.
ety: From bower + -y.
examples: The group performed in the old bowery, an open-air building with a roof of branches laid over vertical poles, the forerunner of the first tabernacle.
This year’s Easter egg hunt will be at the community bowery on Saturday, April 15.

senses: To beat, whack, or attack.
To defeat or humiliate.
ety: Borrowed from Yiddish שלאַנג (shlang, “snake”; by extension, “a penis”) or German Schlange.
examples: He stole your words, calling them expert, schlonging himself on the head with labels, diving into categories.
Please stop insulting, trashing and schlonging your fellow candidates. That's not the Christian, Islamic, Jewish, Hindu or Buddhist thing to do.
His big scrotum would be schlonging off the floor. Wap, wap, wap. Really schlonging.

senses: Of or related to a clan.
Socially exclusive.
ety: From clan + -ish.
examples: Gendrot describes a “clannish” system that ensures officers close ranks to protect their own, leading to a sense of impunity.

senses: One who hurts or does harm.
ety: From hurt + -er.
examples: I shall not be a hurter, if no helper.

senses: Inability to smell; the inability to perceive odors.
ety: From New Latin anosmia, equivalent to an- + -osmi.
examples: Often accompanied by an inability to taste, anosmia occurs abruptly and dramatically in these patients, almost as if a switch had been flipped.

senses: One who provides a briefing.
ety: From brief (verb) + -er (agent noun suffix).
examples: The briefers tried to prove the White House’s case that Iran is shipping deadly weapons, including armor-piercing explosives, to Shiite militias in Iraq.

senses: A trumpet-like wind instrument used in European music of the medieval, Renaissance, and Baroque periods.
An Italian pastry, a kind of croissant.
ety: Borrowed from Italian cornetto, a diminutive of corno (“horn”), from Latin cornū.
examples: A quick espresso, maybe a roll with a little marmalade or a cornetto at the local bar, and then it's off to work or school.

senses: A person who compiles, interprets, or studies statistics.
A mathematician with a specialty of statistics.
ety: From statistic + -ian.
examples: If the F.R. ever expands its administration to include a statistician, his figure for net foot-pounds of elbow grease per trailing ton-mile are going to look quite impressive.

senses: A person who disseminates propaganda.
ety: From propaganda + -ist, after French propagandiste.
examples: It's Alexander the Great who everyone remembers and much of that is down to his and his propagandists' genius.

senses: A type of powdered green tea, traditionally used in Japanese tea ceremonies.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 抹茶 (matcha), from 抹 (matsu, “to wipe, to rub”) + 茶 (cha, “tea”).
examples: And that’s not all – EGCG in matcha can help improve insulin sensitivity, which aids in blood sugar control, and may help to reduce inflammation related to Alzheimer’s disease.

senses: To subject (granular material, especially food grain) to a current of air separating heavier and lighter components, as grain from chaff.
To separate, sift, analyse, or test by separating items having different values.
To blow upon or toss about by blowing; to set in motion as with a fan or wings.
To move about with a flapping motion, as of wings; to flutter.
ety: From Middle English wyndwen, from Old English windwian (“to winnow, fan, ventilate”), from Proto-West Germanic *windwōn, from Proto-Germanic *windwōną, *winþijaną (“to throw about, winnow”), from Proto-Indo-European *wē- (“to winnow, thresh”). Cognate with West Frisian wynje (“to winnow”), dialectal Dutch winden, winnen (“to winnow”), Middle High German winden (“to winnow”), Icelandic vinsa (“to pick out, weed”), Latin vannus (“a winnowing basket”). See fan, van.
examples: By Jacob Behel, of Mifflintown, Pa.,—Improvement in winnowing Machines, Patented August 21, 1847.
They winnowed the field to twelve.
They winnowed the winners from the losers.

senses: Pregnant; carrying developing offspring within one's body.
ety: Shortening of pregnant + -ers.
examples: Michael's troubles may be over soon, except that Christal claims to be preggers with triplets.

senses: Leniency: mercy or forgiveness in the assignment of punishment.
ety: From Latin lēn(iō) (“to soften, soothe”) -i- + -ence, from lēnis (“soft”).
examples: There was lenience in the sentence given by the court, and he got the minimum prison time.

senses: An invisible being of the air.
The elemental being of air, usually female.
A slender woman or girl, usually graceful and sometimes with the implication of sublime station over everyday people.
ety: First attested in 1657. From New Latin sylphes, coined by Paracelsus in the 16th century. The coinage may derive from Latin sylvestris (“of the woods”) and nympha (“nymph”). Ultimately from the root silva (“woods, forest”). Related to sylvan. More at Wikipedia.
examples: Her heart fluttered with expectation—her step was buoyant with hope, and she sprung into the carriage with the lightness of a sylph.
Necromancy meant originally the conjuring up the souls of the dead, and later included the conjuring of all sorts of inhuman spirits such as sylphs, giants, and djinn.

senses: Living with the family of the wife; uxorilocal.
In which newly married couples live with the wife's family.
ety: From matri- + local.
examples: In barring the way, he is enacting a ritual which demands that the new way of patrilocal marriage pay its respect to the more ancient way of matrilocal marriage.

senses: One who holds to particularism.
ety: From particular + -ist, after French particulariste.
examples: On this point there was no difference between mercantilists and feudalists, between crowned planners and vested interests, between centralizing bureaucrats and conservative particularists.

senses: A small stream, a rivulet.
A small artificial channel for water to flow in.
ety: From Middle English runel, rennel, rinel, from Old English rynel (“that which runs; runner; stream”), from Proto-Germanic *runilaz, equivalent to run + -el. Cognate with Scots rinel, rinnal (“stream; runnel”), Swedish rännel (“runner; runnel”).
examples: Spring, is ye comen in, / Dappled larke singe, / Snow melteth, / Runnel pelteth, / Smelleth wind of newe buddinge.
Every little runnel in the bay was astir, and yet the land around him was as dry as flax, and no drop of rain had fallen.

senses: A parasite that lives on the surface of a host organism; such as the Demodex mite, which lives in human hair and eyelashes.
ety: From ecto- (from Ancient Greek ἐκτός (ektós, “outside”)) + parasite.
examples: Ordinarily, allergy to animals is due to either their fine dander which becomes aerosolized or to the exoskeleta, pupae, or feces of their ectoparasites.
You don't need to burrow inside the host: Ectoparasites like you just need to live on the skin.

senses: Tending to worship; showing reverence.
Used as respectful form of address or honorific title for a person or body of persons, now especially in the name of a livery company.
ety: From Middle English worshipful; equivalent to worship + -ful.
examples: Your Worshipful Master has been pleased to speak of me as possessing some powers of speech, but (added his lordship in tones of deep emotion) I have none.

senses: The condition or quality of being instrumental; being useful; serving a purpose.
Something that is instrumental; an instrument.
ety: From instrumental + -ity.
examples: In a later vision the Saviour revealed to her in detail the 'great design' which he wished to establish through her instrumentality.
He spoke of the various instrumentalities which were now employed for the conversion of the world.
Delays and failures will only set her to casting about for new instrumentalities.

senses: A herb of the mint family, Origanum majorana, having aromatic leaves.
The leaves of this plant, especially dried, used in flavouring food.
ety: From Old French majorane, from Medieval Latin maiōrana.
examples: Among the ancients, especially the Romans, marjoram was known to have an aphrodisiac value.

senses: Making a striking or aesthetically pleasing display.
Inclined to showing (by conveying an impression so that events are described in the narrative), instead of telling (by explicitly stating facts).
ety: From show (noun) + -y.
examples: There's a way to make this more showy and less telly. It's like you're in a hurry to get on with the rest of the story.
Six of Crows is very telly and little showy. You are constantly getting info dumps and mini-flashbacks to the characters past.
The ending felt rushed to me, and I wish it would have been more showy and less telly.

senses: Small and cute; pretty in a delicate way; dainty.
ety: From French mignon, from Middle French mignon (“lover, darling, favourite”), from Old French mignon (“dainty, pleasing, gentle, kind”), from Frankish *minnju (“love, friendship, affection, memory”), from Proto-Germanic *minjō (“affectionate thought, care”), from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to think”). Cognate with Old High German minna (“love, care, affection, desire, memory”), Old Saxon minnia (“love”). More at mind. Compare Dutch minnen (“to love”). Doublet of minion.
examples: It was the deep-blue, dreaming, haughty eyes of "Miladi" that he was bringing back to memory, not the brown mignon face that had been so late close to his in the light of the moon.
Starting a dance can be as fortuitous as its termination: a very short, mignon girl asks a tall guy to dance with her, then drops him a moment later without a word.

senses: A lengthy passage in a dramatic or literary work, especially a dull or tedious one; a period of boredom.
ety: Borrowed from French longueur (literally “length”).
examples: Claire Fontaine (who are actually a duo) have queered the phrase, lending its pungency and ambiguity to a biennale that I wish were nearly so succinct. There are longueurs. There are detours and incomprehensible delays.

senses: Pruriently detailed and sensationalistic about something shocking or horrifying, especially with regard to violence or sex.
Melodramatic.
Ghastly, pale, wan in appearance.
Being of a light yellow hue.
ety: Borrowed from Latin lūridus (“pale yellow, wan”).
examples: The accident was described with lurid detail.
Speculating on why publishers rejected it, he wonders whether it was deemed too lurid at the time, especially since Steinbeck was then an unknown author.
Fierce o'er their beauty blazed the lurid flame;

senses: A Chinese dumpling, often stuffed with varieties of meat or seafood and vegetables.
ety: Borrowed from Cantonese 雲吞 /云吞 (wan⁴ tan¹, wan⁴ tan⁴).
examples: The wonton will be done when the crab filling is cooked through and the wonton are very soft.
When the water boils again, the wonton are ready to be inhaled with a little chicken broth.
Arrange cooked or uncooked filled wonton in a single layer on a baking sheet. Cover and place in freezer. When the wonton are frozen, transfer to freezer bag.

senses: To greet in French with "bonjour".
ety: Borrowed from French bonjour (“good afternoon/good day/good morning”).
examples: He went on down the boulevard, bonjouring right and left, lifting his hat, bowing. He moved very slowly.
Connaughton entered the simple but cheery restaurant, checked his coat, bonjoured the maître d'...
They bonjoured back and stood there awkwardly. Finally, Flood broke the silence.

senses: Reasoning, conscious deliberate inference; the activity or process of reasoning.
Thought or reasoning that is exact, valid and rational.
A proposition arrived at by such thought.
ety: Borrowed from French ratiocination, from Latin ratiōcinātiō (“argumentation, reasoning, ratiocination; a syllogism”), from ratiōcinātus (“reckoned”) + -tiō (suffix forming a noun relating to some action or the result of an action). Ratiōcinātus is the perfect passive participle of ratiōcinor (“to compute, reckon; to argue, infer”), from ratiō (“reason, explanation”) (from reor (“to calculate, reckon”), possibly from Proto-Italic *rēōr, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂reh₁- (“to put in order”)) + -cinor, modelled after vāticinor (“to foretell, prophesy”), equivalent to ratiocinate + -ion.
examples: It is hard to follow the kinks of woman suffrage ratiocination.

senses: Cute, adorable or beautiful.
ety: Semantic extension from Malay jambu, which originated from Sanskrit जम्बु (jambu, “a fruit or a blood pear”).
examples: She has this healthy glow, almost like she's golden skinned, but oh so jambu lah!
Add me pls . There are only 5 Salmah Samions ! The most jambu looking profile is me lah !
I also wanna look jambu also what on that 2-day event.

senses: A low, hand-operated truck, generally with four wheels, used for transporting objects or for riding on as a toy; a trolley.
One of two sets of wheels under a locomotive or railcar; also, a structure with axles and wheels under a locomotive, railcar, or semi which provides support and reduces vibration for the vehicle.
A railway carriage.
A soapbox racing vehicle.
ety: A dialectal word from Northern England of unknown origin which is unrelated to bogey (“hostile supernatural creature; terrifying thing, bugbear”).
examples: The bogie coaches which he spoke of last year had been brought or were being brought into active service, but they had no further wagon stock available.
Hard work is required from men and machines as I was to experience later when footplating Lambton No 5 on five bogies battling its way up Newtondale.

senses: A small, informal Italian-style restaurant.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from Italian trattoria.
examples: La Granita is a new trattoria on the Upper East Side with a charcoal grill, a rotisserie and a wood-burning pizza oven.

senses: A simple wooden harp or zither used in central and eastern Africa.
ety: From Acholi naŋa.
examples: The "shoulder harp" or "nanga" had a boat-shaped sound chest.
The nanga of Nubia is similar; here also, long wooden pegs prevent the strings from slipping.
The artist uses his voice, he sings his laws to the accompaniment of the nanga, the harp; he twists his body to the rhythm of the drums, to proclaim his rules.

senses: A person (especially a male) who débuts, or appears for the first time.
ety: From French débutant, equivalent to debut + -ant.
examples: The Australian batsmen were expecting an easier time with debutants Lonwabo Tsotsobe (4-50) and Wayne Parnell (1-52) replacing Dale Steyn and Ntini, while allrounder Kallis was also rested.

senses: A fruit or pod of a carob tree (Ceratonia siliqua).
examples: Among other articles, they brought with them a great quantity of locusts, which are a kind of pulse, sweet and pleasant to the palate, and in shape resembling French beans, but longer.

senses: Low moral standards.
Political corruption.
A person of low moral standards.
A man who is sexually aggressive or forward with women to the point of causing disgust.
Sleazy material or publications.
ety: Back-formation from sleazy, originally used to describe the thinness and low quality of cloth.
examples: The level of sleaze in this city seems to have been rising rapidly in recent years.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage is facing an investigation by the Commons sleaze watchdog over a £5m (€5.7m) gift from a party donor.
She knew that sleaze Hakido would do something to stick the knife in and twist it to the hilt.

senses: A quantity of the stalks and ears of wheat, rye, or other grain, bound together; a bundle of grain or straw.
Any collection of things bound together.
A bundle of arrows sufficient to fill a quiver, or the allowance of each archer.
A quantity of arrows, usually twenty-four.
ety: From Middle English scheef, from Old English sċēaf, from Proto-West Germanic *skaub, from Proto-Germanic *skauba- (“sheaf”). Cognates Akin to West Frisian skeaf (“sheaf”), Dutch schoof (“sheaf”), German Schaub, Old Norse skauf (“a fox's tail”). Compare further Gothic 𐍃𐌺𐌿𐍆𐍄 (skuft, “hair of the head”), German Schopf (“tuft”).
examples: O, let me teach you how to knit again This scattered corn into one mutual sheaf, These broken limbs again into one body.
And then in haste her bow'r she leaves, With Thestylis to bind the sheaves; Or if the earlier season lead To the tann'd haycock in the mead.
Ev’n while the Reaper fills his greedy hands, / And binds the golden Sheafs in brittle bands

senses: The domination of a field of endeavour by two entities or people.
ety: From duo- (prefix meaning ‘two’) + -poly (suffix meaning ‘pertaining to the number of sellers in a market’), by analogy with monopoly.
examples: In Spain, Socialist and PP governments have alternated since the 1980s. This cosy duopoly was weakened by the long recession that followed the bursting of Spain’s housing bubble in 2007.
First past the post voting has long maintained American politics as an effective duopoly where power simply alternates between two main parties.

senses: A holy candelabrum with seven branches used in the Temple of Jerusalem.
A candelabrum with nine branches, used in Jewish worship on Hanukkah.
ety: Borrowed from Hebrew מְנוֹרָה (m'norá). From the same Proto-Semitic root *nūr- (“light”) as minaret.
examples: My father brings home a big brass antique menorah, shaped like an archway, heavy, on a pedestal, on a round base.
In America every December my mother had decorated our home with metal Stars of David she hung on strings in the doorways and lit the menorah as we gathered at the table.
However, traditional Sefardi families follow the halacha that each household uses only one menorah lit by the head of the household, to represent everyone in unison.

senses: The study of structures of consciousness as experienced from the first-person point of view.
A movement based on this, originated about 1905 by Edmund Husserl.
ety: From phenomenon + -logy, from Ancient Greek φαινόμενον (phainómenon, “thing appearing to view”), hence "the study of what shows itself (to consciousness)". According to Martin Heidegger's Introduction to Phenomenological Research, "the expression “phenomenology” first appears in the eighteenth century in Christian Wolff’s School, in Lambert’s Neues Organon, in connection with analogous developments popular at the time, like dianoiology and alethiology, and means a theory of illusion, a doctrine for avoiding illusion." (p.3)
examples: Writing, individuation, and civilization are all parts of one larger cultural phenomenology.

The process of questioning back displaces the emphasis in phenomenology from an inquiry into modes of givenness, which assumes that there can be a simple starting point, to an inquiry into modes of pregivenness.
